learningObjectives.text: Identify the central source-grounded idea in Achilles: Anger and Honor.
Connect the idea to the cited source, genre, and version.

iliad.author: Homer
iliad.excerpt: mother Thetis to ask Jove to help the Trojans—Scene between Jove and Juno on Olympus. Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for
iliad.note: Verbatim local text with whitespace normalized. Lesson analysis is interpretation, not part of this quotation.

narrativeBlocks.title: A poem about one crisis
narrativeBlocks.body: The Iliad begins with Achilles’ anger, not with Troy’s origins or the Wooden Horse. That narrows the poem into an intense study of honor, withdrawal, and consequence.

narrativeBlocks.title: Greatness without safety
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotations are available under the source buttons. They are translations, not the lesson author’s wording. Compare the work and locator before drawing conclusions.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read the opening as a thesis
narrativeBlocks.body: The first lines point toward rage and its human cost, shaping what the poem wants us to notice about heroism.

narrativeBlocks.title: Honor is a system, not just a feeling
narrativeBlocks.body: The insult matters because heroic status is publicly assigned and publicly removed. Track who loses honor, who enforces the loss, and which community pays for it.

narrativeBlocks.title: Keep the epic lens
narrativeBlocks.body: Read Achilles here through the Iliad alone. Later traditions may smooth him into a simpler warrior, but this poem deliberately begins with a wound to status and the damage that follows.

quiz.prompt: What does Achilles withdraw from after the quarrel?
quiz.explanation: Fighting for the Achaean army. Revisit the named passage and distinguish its narrative from the lesson’s interpretation.

quiz.prompt: Why is anger not merely private here?

choices.text: It never affects any other character.
It concerns only a footrace at Olympia.
Its consequences fall on the fighting community.
